teile.einleitung: Many animal and plant species do not live in one single large group, but spread over many small habitats. When these groups are linked by migration, we speak of a metapopulation. The concept helps in nature conservation.
wichtigste: A metapopulation consists of spatially separate subpopulations that are linked by migration.
The term was coined by Richard Levins in 1969.
Subpopulations can die out and later be settled anew.
Immigrants can save a small subpopulation from dying out: the rescue effect.
A subpopulation that would die out without immigration is called a sink.
In Switzerland, wildlife overpasses link separated habitats again.

abschnitte.text: A **population** is a group of living things of the same species in one place. Often suitable habitats such as ponds, meadows or patches of woodland are scattered across the landscape like islands. On each island lives a **subpopulation**. Individual animals travel from patch to patch. All the subpopulations together form a **metapopulation**, a “population of populations”.

The ecologist **Richard Levins** described metapopulations in 1969 with a simple formula. Here e is the rate at which subpopulations die out, and c is the rate at which empty patches are settled anew. At equilibrium, the share of occupied patches is **p = 1 minus e/c**. With e = 0.2 and c = 0.5, p = 1 minus 0.4 = **0.6**. So six out of ten patches are occupied.

The Finnish researcher **Ilkka Hanski** studied the **Glanville fritillary** on the **Åland Islands** for decades. There the butterflies live on many small meadows. Hanski showed that individual groups keep disappearing while others appear anew. The species survives as long as enough meadows can be reached.

In the **mainland-island model** there is one large, stable main population that supplies the small subpopulations around it with immigrants. A subpopulation that has more young than needed is called a **source**. One that would die out without constant immigration is called a **sink**. When immigrants strengthen a shrinking group, this is called the **rescue effect**.

Roads, settlements and railway lines cut up the landscape. Animals such as deer, foxes or amphibians then can no longer reach other groups. In Switzerland, **wildlife overpasses** are therefore built over motorways and **wildlife corridors** are set aside. In this way separated subpopulations are linked again, and the metapopulation stays viable.

gewusst: A species can survive in a landscape even though each of its subpopulations will sooner or later die out.
Even small ponds lying close together can work like a network of stepping stones for frogs and newts.

teile.einleitung: Mercury is the planet closest to the Sun, and at the same time the smallest planet in our Solar System. It races around the Sun once in only 88 days. On its surface, glowing heat and icy cold take turns.
wichtigste: Mercury is the planet closest to the Sun.
It is the smallest of the eight planets in the Solar System.
It needs only 88 days for one trip around the Sun.
Mercury has no moon and almost no atmosphere.
In the day it gets over 400 degrees hot, at night far below minus 150 degrees cold.
Its surface is covered with craters and looks similar to our Moon.
It is named after Mercury, the swift messenger of the gods in Roman legend.

abschnitte.text: Mercury is the first planet from the Sun and is one of the **rocky planets**. With a diameter of about 4,900 kilometres it is the smallest planet in the Solar System, only a little bigger than our Moon. It has a very large **iron core** that makes up a large part of its interior. It got its name from the Roman messenger of the gods Mercury, because it moves so quickly across the sky.

Mercury goes around the Sun in only **88 days**, faster than any other planet. It turns on its own axis very slowly, though, once in about 59 Earth days. As a result, a whole day from one sunrise to the next lasts about 176 Earth days. So on Mercury a day is twice as long as a year.

Because Mercury has almost no **atmosphere**, it cannot hold on to heat. On the day side it gets over 400 degrees hot, hot enough to melt lead. On the night side the temperature falls to about minus 170 degrees. In deep craters at the poles, where sunlight never falls, researchers have even discovered **water ice**.

The surface of Mercury is grey and covered with countless **craters**, like the surface of the Moon. The biggest known impact crater is the **Caloris Basin**, about 1,500 kilometres across. Long steep slopes run for hundreds of kilometres; they probably formed when the planet shrank as it cooled. Many craters are named after famous artists, musicians and writers.

Because Mercury is so close to the Sun, it is hard to reach with space probes. The American probe Mariner 10 was the first to fly past it, in the 1970s. The probe **MESSENGER** orbited it from 2011 to 2015 and mapped the whole surface. The European-Japanese mission **BepiColombo** launched in 2018 and is due to enter orbit around Mercury at the end of 2026.

From Earth, Mercury is hard to see, because it always stands close to the Sun. You can only spot it briefly after sunset in the evening sky or shortly before sunrise in the morning sky, low above the horizon. Sometimes Mercury, seen from Earth, passes exactly in front of the Sun’s disc; this is called a **transit of Mercury**. The next transit of Mercury can be seen in November 2032.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large heavenly body that orbits a star such as the Sun.
The envelope of gas that surrounds a planet.
When Mercury, seen from Earth, passes in front of the Sun.
An unmanned spacecraft that explores other heavenly bodies.

gewusst: Although Mercury is closest to the Sun, Venus is the hottest planet, because its dense atmosphere holds in the heat.
On Mercury, at some places you can see the Sun rise briefly, set again and rise again.
Mercury is smaller than the biggest moons of Jupiter and Saturn, Ganymede and Titan.

teile.einleitung: The ox-eye daisy is a well-known meadow flower with white petals and a yellow centre. In early summer, whole fields of ox-eye daisies shine on many meadows.
wichtigste: The ox-eye daisy has white petals and a yellow centre.
The centre is made up of many tiny tubular flowers.
It looks like a big daisy.
It grows to about 30 to 60 centimetres tall.
Ox-eye daisies bloom mainly in May and June.
In Switzerland people often say “Margritli”.

abschnitte.text: The **ox-eye daisy** has a ring of long, **white** petals and a **yellow centre**. It looks very like the small **daisy**, but is much bigger and has a long stem. It grows to about **30 to 60 centimetres** tall and stands well above the grass.

What looks like a single flower is really very many. The yellow centre is made of very many tiny **tubular flowers**. The white “petals” at the edge are also little flowers. Together they form a **flower head**. That is why the ox-eye daisy belongs to the **daisy family**.

Ox-eye daisies bloom mainly in **May and June**, often later in summer too. They like **poor meadows** that get little fertiliser. There they have enough light and room. The open flower is easy to reach. That is why many **beetles, flies and bees** land on it.

In Switzerland the ox-eye daisy is often lovingly called **“Margritli”**. The first name **Margrit** comes from the same word. Children like to play a counting game with the ox-eye daisy: they **pluck** one petal after another and say a line in turn. The last petal decides the result.

gewusst: The name Margerite, as the plant is known in German, comes from the Greek word for pearl.
The sunflower and the dandelion are also members of the daisy family.

teile.einleitung: Sequoias are huge conifers from California. They are among the largest and oldest living things on Earth, and today they also grow in Swiss parks.
wichtigste: The giant sequoia comes from the Sierra Nevada in California.
Sequoias are conifers with scale-like needles and cones.
Giant sequoias grow over 80 metres tall and live for over 3000 years.
The thick, reddish-brown bark protects them from forest fires.
The cones are only about as big as a hen’s egg.
The tallest tree in the world is a coast redwood.

abschnitte.text: The **giant sequoia** grows wild on the mountain slopes of the **Sierra Nevada** in **California** in the USA. It is a **conifer**: it has small, scale-like needles and bears cones. The biggest giant sequoias are **over 80 metres** tall. Their trunks are so thick at the bottom that many people would have to link arms to reach around them.
The oldest giant sequoias are **over 3000 years** old. That makes them some of the oldest living things on Earth. Some were already standing when emperors still ruled in ancient Rome.

The **bark** of the giant sequoia is fibrous, soft and **reddish brown**. That is why the trunks glow red in the sun. It can grow more than half a metre thick and does not burn easily. In this way the trees survive many **forest fires**.
Although the tree is huge, its **cones** are small. They are only about 5 to 8 centimetres long, roughly as big as a **hen’s egg**. The seeds inside are tiny.

Around **1850**, the first seeds came from California to Europe. Soon afterwards, sequoias were also planted in Switzerland, in **parks** and gardens. So they have been growing here for over 150 years. A close relative is the **coast redwood**. It is the tallest tree in the world: the tallest known tree in California is over **115 metres** tall.

gewusst: The giant sequoia is one of the trees with the greatest volume of wood in the world.
Fire even helps the cones to open and release their seeds.

teile.einleitung: Mangroves are forests of trees and shrubs that grow in salt water on tropical coasts. At high tide they stand in the sea, at low tide in mud.
wichtigste: Mangroves can cope with salty sea water.
At high tide they are flooded, at low tide the ground dries out.
Many mangroves get air through breathing roots.
On Borneo, the proboscis monkey lives in mangroves.
Male fiddler crabs wave one big claw.

abschnitte.text: Most plants die if they get salty water. **Mangroves** can live with it. They grow on flat, warm coasts in the **tropics**, often at river mouths. Some species keep the salt back at the roots, others get rid of it again through their leaves.

At **high tide** the sea rises and floods the mangroves. At **low tide** the ground dries out again. The muddy ground contains hardly any oxygen. That is why many mangroves grow **stilt roots**, which hold them in the soft ground, and **breathing roots**, which stick out of the mud and take in air.
On the island of **Borneo**, the **proboscis monkey** lives in mangroves and in forests along rivers. It has a very large nose and is a good **swimmer**. It eats mainly leaves.
Many **crabs** live on the mud of the mangroves. In the **fiddler crab**, the male has one very large claw. He waves it as if he were greeting someone. The other claw is small.

Between the roots of the mangroves, many young **fish** find shelter from enemies. Mangroves hold the mud in place and protect the **coast** from waves and storms. That is why they are important for people and animals.

gewusst: Mangrove forests are found on the coasts of many tropical countries in Asia, Africa and the Americas.

teile.einleitung: The Milky Way is our home galaxy, a huge collection of stars, gas and dust. Our Sun and the Earth belong to it too. On dark nights you can see it as a bright, milky band across the sky.
wichtigste: The Milky Way is the galaxy that our Solar System belongs to.
It has the shape of a spiral with several arms.
There are estimated to be 100 to 400 billion stars in the Milky Way.
Its diameter is about 100,000 light years or more.
The Sun lies in a spiral arm, about 26,000 light years from the centre.
At the centre is a huge black hole.
Because of light pollution, the Milky Way can hardly be seen in cities any more.

abschnitte.text: A **galaxy** is a huge collection of stars held together by gravity. Our galaxy is called the Milky Way. Besides billions of stars, it contains clouds of gas, dust and planets. In the Universe there are billions more galaxies.

The Milky Way is a **spiral galaxy**: seen from above, it would look like a flat, glowing wheel with curved arms. To be more precise, it has a long bar in the middle, so it is a barred spiral galaxy. Its diameter is about 100,000 light years or more. A **light year** is the distance that light travels in a year, which is almost 10 trillion kilometres.

Our Sun does not lie at the centre, but in a spiral arm, about 26,000 light years from the middle. The Sun and its planets orbit the centre of the Milky Way. It needs about 230 million years for one lap. The last time the Sun was in the same place, the first dinosaurs were living on Earth.

abschnitte.titel: The heart of the Milky Way
abschnitte.text: At the centre of the Milky Way sits a **black hole** called Sagittarius A*. It is about four million times as heavy as the Sun. You cannot see it directly, but stars orbit around it very fast. In 2022 a first picture of its surroundings was published.

Because we sit in the middle of the flat disc, we see the Milky Way from the side as a bright band across the sky. In summer the brightest part, towards the constellation Sagittarius, is easy to see. Around 1610, Galileo Galilei realised with his telescope that the milky band is made up of countless individual stars. In Switzerland you see it best far from cities, for example in the mountains or in the Gantrisch Nature Park, where people fight **light pollution**.

The name comes from a Greek legend in which milk from the goddess Hera was splashed across the sky. The word galaxy also comes from the Greek word for milk. The Milky Way belongs to the **Local Group**, together with the Andromeda Galaxy and many smaller galaxies. In a few billion years, the Milky Way and Andromeda will probably merge.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge collection of billions of stars, gas and dust.
The distance light travels in a year, almost 10 trillion kilometres.
A curved arm of a spiral galaxy, rich in stars.
Artificial light that brightens the night sky and hides the stars.

gewusst: Light from the other end of the Milky Way takes tens of thousands of years to reach us.
The Andromeda Galaxy is about 2.5 million light years away and can be seen with the naked eye.
Nobody has ever seen the Milky Way from outside; all pictures of it are drawings or models.

teile.einleitung: Ladybirds are small, round beetles with bright wing cases and black spots. They eat aphids and are seen as bringers of good luck.
wichtigste: The seven-spot ladybird is the best known in Switzerland.
The number of spots shows the species, not the age.
Beetles and larvae eat very many aphids.
When in danger, the ladybird gives off a yellow, bitter fluid.
The red colour warns birds.
In winter, many ladybirds often hide together.

abschnitte.text: The best known here is the **seven-spot ladybird**. It has red **wing cases** with **seven** black spots. But there are many other species with other colours and numbers of spots. The number of spots depends on the **species**. It does not show the age and does not change as the beetle gets older.

Ladybirds like to eat **aphids**. Their **larvae** also eat very many of them. The larvae look quite different from the beetles: they are long, dark and often have pale patches. Because they gobble up aphids, ladybirds are very welcome in the garden. That is why they are called **beneficial insects**.

The red colour is a **warning**. It tells birds: I do not taste good. That is why they rarely eat ladybirds. When in danger, the ladybird also gives off a **yellow, bitter fluid** from its legs. It often plays dead too.
In autumn, ladybirds look for sheltered hiding places, such as **crevices**, leaves or gaps in walls. Often **many lie together** there. In spring, when it gets warmer, they come out again.
The ladybird is a popular **lucky charm**. In German it is also called the **Glückskäfer**, the “lucky beetle”. It is often pictured on New Year or birthday cards.

gewusst: A single ladybird larva can eat hundreds of aphids during its development.
The harlequin ladybird was introduced into Europe and is now also widespread in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The mango tree is a large evergreen tree from the tropics. Its sweet, juicy fruit, the mango, is popular all over the world.
wichtigste: The mango is the national fruit of India.
Mango trees can grow over 30 metres tall.
The tree is evergreen and has leaves all year round.
In the middle of the mango is a large, flat stone.
Mango and cashew belong to the same plant family.
Mango trees can live for over 100 years.

abschnitte.text: The mango has been grown in **India** for thousands of years. There it is the **national fruit**. Today mango trees grow in many warm countries around the world. In India **lassi** is also popular, a drink made from yoghurt. **Mango lassi** is a well-known kind.

Mango trees can grow very large and reach **over 30 metres**. On plantations they are usually kept smaller so that the fruit is easier to pick. The mango tree is **evergreen**: it never drops all its leaves at once and has leaves all year round. Mango trees live a long time. Some still bear fruit after **more than 100 years**.

The mango is a **stone fruit**. In its middle is a large, **flat stone**. Ripe mangoes have juicy, **yellow to orange** flesh. The skin can be green, yellow or red. So the colour of the skin does not always show whether a mango is ripe.
Mango and **cashew** belong to the same plant family, the **sumac family**. The pistachio also belongs to this family. You cannot tell from looking at the fruit, but the plants are closely related.

gewusst: There are very many different kinds of mango, with different shapes, colours and sweetness.

teile.einleitung: A meteor, also called a shooting star, is a short flash of light in the night sky. It happens when a piece of rock from space enters the atmosphere at high speed and burns up there. If you look up at the sky on a clear August night, you can often see many shooting stars.
wichtigste: A meteor is a piece of rock that burns up in the atmosphere, and is also called a shooting star.
The piece of rock in space is called a meteoroid.
If a remnant of it reaches the ground, it is called a meteorite.
Most shooting stars come from particles smaller than a grain of sand.
Meteors usually light up at a height of about 80 to 120 kilometres.
In a meteor shower such as the Perseids in August, you see especially many shooting stars.
An especially bright meteor is called a fireball or bolide.

abschnitte.text: The term **meteor** really means the streak of light in the sky; in everyday speech we talk about a shooting star. But it has nothing to do with stars. It is caused by a small piece of rock or metal from space, a **meteoroid**. If a remnant of it falls to Earth, it is called a **meteorite**.

Meteoroids race into the Earth’s **atmosphere** at 11 to 72 kilometres per second. The air in front of them is squeezed and heated so strongly that the particle vaporises and makes the air all around it glow. This usually happens at a height of 80 to 120 kilometres, far above the clouds and aircraft. Most shooting stars come from particles smaller than a **grain of sand**.

Several times a year, the Earth flies through a trail of dust that a **comet** has left behind on its path. Then you see especially many shooting stars, which all seem to come from the same direction of the sky; this is called a **meteor shower**. The best known are the **Perseids** around 12 August, which come from the comet Swift-Tuttle. In December the Geminids follow, which often provide just as many shooting stars.

Bigger lumps produce especially bright meteors, which are called **fireballs** or bolides and sometimes burst with a bang. In February 2013, a lump about 20 metres across exploded over the Russian city of Chelyabinsk and shattered thousands of window panes. Very rarely, large bodies hit the Earth and leave craters such as the Barringer Crater in Arizona. About 66 million years ago, a huge impact helped to wipe out the dinosaurs.

In Switzerland only a few meteorites have been found so far. The best-known site is the **Twannberg** above Lake Biel, where many pieces of an iron meteorite have been found since 1984. Today **camera networks** run by experts and amateur astronomers watch the sky over Switzerland and help to calculate where meteorites have fallen. Meteorites are valuable for research because they contain material from the time the Solar System formed.

To watch them you do not need a telescope, just a dark place far from city lights and a little patience. The best thing is to lie down comfortably and let your eyes get used to the dark for about 20 minutes. After midnight you usually see more shooting stars, because the Earth is then turning in the direction of its flight. According to an old **custom**, you may make a wish when you see a shooting star.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small lump of rock or metal flying through space.
The remnant of a meteoroid that has reached the ground.
Many shooting stars that come at the same time from the same direction of the sky.
An especially bright meteor, also called a bolide.

gewusst: Every day, tonnes of tiny dust particles fall from space onto the Earth.
The Perseids are named that because their shooting stars seem to come from the constellation Perseus.
A shooting star usually shines for less than a second.

teile.einleitung: Mendel’s laws describe how characteristics are passed on from parents to offspring. The monk Gregor Mendel found them through crossing experiments with peas. They are among the foundations of the study of heredity, genetics.
wichtigste: Gregor Mendel published his results in 1866.
Law of uniformity: if you cross two pure-bred parents, all the offspring of the F1 generation are the same.
Law of segregation: in the F2 generation of a dominant-recessive inheritance, the characteristics appear in the ratio 3 to 1.
The genotypes of the F2 generation are distributed 1 AA to 2 Aa to 1 aa.
Law of independent assortment: with two characteristics, the F2 generation splits in the ratio 9 to 3 to 3 to 1.
One exception is gene linkage: genes on the same chromosome are often inherited together.

abschnitte.text: **Gregor Mendel** lived in the 19th century as a monk in the monastery in Brno, in what is now the Czech Republic. In the monastery garden he crossed **pea plants** with different characteristics for many years, such as yellow and green seeds. He counted the offspring carefully and worked with number ratios. His work was hardly noticed for a long time. Only around **1900** did other researchers rediscover it.

Each characteristic is determined by two **hereditary factors**, one from each parent. They are written with letters, for example A and a. A capital letter stands for a **dominant** factor, which wins out. A small letter stands for a **recessive** factor, which only shows if it is present twice. **Pure-bred** means AA or aa, **hybrid** means Aa. The hereditary factors are called the **genotype**, and the visible characteristic the **phenotype** or appearance.

If you cross two hybrid plants Aa times Aa, you get AA, Aa, aA and aa. Three out of four show the dominant characteristic, so **3 to 1**. For the genotypes the result is **1 to 2 to 1**. If you look at two characteristics at the same time, they combine freely: (3 to 1) times (3 to 1) gives **9 to 3 to 3 to 1**. The genotype aabb occurs in only **1 of 16** offspring.

A plant with the dominant characteristic can be AA or Aa. To find out which, you cross it with a **pure-bred recessive** partner aa. This is called a **backcross** or **test cross**. If the plant is Aa, the offspring show both characteristics in the ratio **1 to 1**. If it is AA, all the offspring look the same.

A factor does not always win out completely. In the **four o’clock flower**, the offspring of a red and a white pure-bred plant bloom **pink**. This is called **intermediate inheritance**. Also, the law of independent assortment only applies to genes that lie on different chromosomes. If they lie on the same chromosome, this is called **gene linkage**.

gewusst: In his experiments, Mendel studied many thousands of pea plants.
The word “gene” did not yet exist in Mendel’s time. It was only introduced at the start of the 20th century.

teile.einleitung: Maize is a large cereal plant that originally comes from the Americas. Its kernels are used to make popcorn, polenta, cornflakes and animal feed.
wichtigste: The kernels sit in rows on the cob.
Most maize kernels are yellow, but there are also white, red and blue ones.
Maize was grown in Mexico thousands of years ago.
A maize plant often grows taller than 2 metres.
In Ticino, polenta is cooked from maize semolina.
Popcorn maize bursts open into popcorn when it is heated.

abschnitte.text: On maize, the kernels sit in rows on the **cob**. The cob is wrapped in green leaves, and fine threads stick out at the top. Most kernels are **yellow**. But there are also varieties with white, red or blue kernels.

Maize comes from the **Americas**. People were already growing it in **Mexico** thousands of years ago. After the discovery of America, sailors brought it to **Europe**. Today maize is grown all over the world, including in Switzerland.

Maize grows quickly in summer and often reaches **over 2 metres**, which is taller than a person. To stop it falling over, it grows **prop roots** at the bottom of the stalk. You cannot see into a field of maize. In summer, some farmers cut paths into it and turn it into a **maize maze**, where you have to find the way out.

**Popcorn maize** has a little water locked inside. When the kernel is heated, the water turns to steam and the kernel bursts open: that is how **popcorn** is made. To make **cornflakes**, maize is cooked, rolled flat and toasted. The English word “corn” means maize here.

**Polenta** is a porridge made from **maize semolina**. In **Ticino** it is a well-known dish and is often eaten with meat, mushrooms or cheese. In Switzerland a lot of maize is also grown as **feed** for cows.

gewusst: Maize belongs to the sweet grasses, like wheat and rice.
A single maize cob often carries several hundred kernels.

teile.einleitung: In the garden, not all plants have to grow in separate rows. In companion planting, different species are put side by side on purpose. Good neighbours can help each other.
wichtigste: In companion planting, different plant species grow together in one bed.
Onions next to carrots can distract the carrot fly.
The “three sisters” of the milpa are maize, beans and squash.
Marigolds can push back harmful roundworms in the soil.
Deep-rooted and shallow-rooted plants use different layers of soil.
The opposite is monoculture, where only one plant species grows.

abschnitte.text: **Companion planting** means that different plant species grow together in one bed. A well-known pair is **carrots** and **onions**. The smell of the onions can confuse the **carrot fly**, whose larvae eat carrots. In return, carrots are said to distract the onion fly. Between **tomatoes**, **basil** is often planted, which has similar needs for warmth and water.

In Central America, farmers have grown the **milpa** for a very long time. There **maize**, **beans** and **squash** grow together, the “three sisters”. The maize serves as a **climbing frame** for the beans. With the help of bacteria on their roots, the beans can fix **nitrogen** from the air and so improve the soil. The big leaves of the squash shade the ground, keep it damp and suppress weeds.

The **marigold** is often planted among vegetables. Its roots give off substances that can push back harmful **roundworms** in the soil. Roundworms, also called nematodes, are tiny worms that suck at roots. Flowering plants also attract useful insects such as bees and hoverflies.

Plants root to different depths. Lettuce has rather shallow roots, other vegetables reach deeper. When **deep-rooted and shallow-rooted** plants grow side by side, they use **different layers of soil**. So they compete less for water and nutrients. The space in the bed is used better.

The opposite of companion planting is **monoculture**. Here only plants of one species grow over large areas, for example only maize or only wheat. This is easier to farm with machines. But pests and diseases can spread more easily. Mixed plantings are seen as more varied, but need more hand work and knowledge.

gewusst: The milpa has been grown in Central America for several thousand years.
Not all plants are good neighbours: some hold back each other’s growth.

teile.einleitung: In the water of streams, rivers and lakes, tiny amounts of medicines, pesticides and other chemicals are found. They are called micropollutants. Even at very low concentrations they can harm water animals.
wichtigste: Micropollutants are substances that can cause harm even at very low concentrations.
They usually occur in the range of nanograms to micrograms per litre.
Conventional sewage treatment plants remove them poorly, because bacteria can hardly break them down.
Switzerland is equipping selected sewage treatment plants with an additional cleaning stage.
This stage is meant to remove about 80 per cent of the micropollutants.
The ARA Neugut in Dübendorf was the first sewage treatment plant in Switzerland to use ozonation in full operation.

abschnitte.text: Micropollutants come from many sources: from **medicines**, **pesticides**, cosmetics, cleaning products and industrial chemicals. A well-known example is the painkiller **diclofenac**. Part of the active ingredient leaves the body again and gets into the sewage treatment plant with the waste water. Pesticides, on the other hand, are often washed from fields into streams by the rain.

The substances occur in **nanograms to micrograms per litre**. A nanogram is a billionth of a gram, a microgram a millionth of a gram. An example: a river contains 200 nanograms of a medicine per litre. A cubic metre has 1,000 litres, so that makes 200,000 nanograms. That is **200 micrograms** per cubic metre. Even with such small amounts, fish, crayfish or water insects can be harmed.

abschnitte.titel: The limits of the sewage plant
abschnitte.text: In an ordinary **sewage treatment plant** (ARA), **bacteria** break down dirt and nutrients. But many micropollutants are **hard for bacteria to break down** and flow on almost unchanged into the waters. That is why extra processes are needed. In **ozonation**, the substances are broken up with the gas ozone. In treatment with **activated carbon**, they stick to tiny particles of carbon.

Switzerland has decided to upgrade selected large sewage treatment plants with an **additional cleaning stage**. The aim is to remove **about 80 per cent** of the micropollutants. The first to put ozonation into full operation was the **ARA Neugut** in **Dübendorf**. The upgrade is paid for mainly through a **waste water charge**, which is collected per connected person.

**Groundwater**, which supplies a large part of our drinking water, can also be affected. The fungicide **chlorothalonil** was used against fungal diseases on fields. Its breakdown products turned up in groundwater in many places. The substance was then **banned** in Switzerland. Cases like this show how long substances can stay in water.

gewusst: Modern measuring devices can still detect individual substances when only a few nanograms of them are in a litre of water.
Ozone is the same gas that, high up in the atmosphere, protects the Earth from UV radiation.

teile.einleitung: The mole is a small mammal that spends almost its whole life underground. Everyone knows its molehills on meadows and in gardens.
wichtigste: The mole lives in tunnels under the ground.
It eats mainly earthworms and insect larvae, not plants.
It digs with broad, spade-like front paws.
It sees very badly, but smells and feels very well.
It does not hibernate.
Without its tail it is about 11 to 16 centimetres long.

abschnitte.text: The **mole** almost always lives in its **tunnels** under the ground. It only rarely comes up to the surface. It is about **11 to 16 centimetres** long, plus a short tail of 2 to 4 centimetres. Its short, **black fur** is as soft as velvet. It can be stroked in any direction, so the mole can get forwards and backwards through the narrow tunnels.

The mole’s **front paws** are as broad as **spades** and have strong claws. With them it pushes the soil aside. It pushes the rest of the soil up out of the ground. That is how **molehills** are made.
It is dark underground. The mole’s **eyes** are tiny, and it sees only very badly. But it can **smell** and **feel** very well. Its sensitive snout picks up the smallest movements.
The mole eats **no plants**. It catches **earthworms** and **insect larvae** in its tunnels. It does not **hibernate**. In winter it digs deeper, because that is where the worms live then.

Many molehills on a meadow annoy **farmers**. When mowing and making hay, the soil from the hills gets mixed into the grass. **Dirty feed** is bad for the animals. In the garden, on the other hand, the mole loosens the soil and eats the larvae of pests.

gewusst: The mole is more closely related to the hedgehog and the shrews than to mice.
A mole can dig many metres of new tunnels in a short time.

teile.einleitung: The **spring snowflake** is one of the first flowers of the year. It often blooms as early as March, when it is still cool in the woods. With its little white bells it looks pretty and delicate. In German it is called the “Märzenbecher”, the “March cup”.
wichtigste: The spring snowflake often starts to bloom in March.
Its flowers are white.
At the tips of the petals there are green or yellow spots.
All six petals are the same length.
It likes to grow in damp woods.
Another German name is “Frühlings-Knotenblume”.

abschnitte.text: The flower of the spring snowflake is **white** and hangs down like a little bell. It has six petals. At each **tip** there is a small **green or yellow spot**. A stem usually carries **one or two flowers**. The flowers have a light scent. The plant grows to about the height of a hand or a little more.

The spring snowflake looks like the **snowdrop**. But you can easily tell the two apart. In the spring snowflake **all the petals are the same length**. In the snowdrop the three outer petals are long and the three inner ones short. Another German name for the spring snowflake is **“Frühlings-Knotenblume”**.

The spring snowflake likes to grow in **damp woods**, in floodplains and on stream banks. There the soil is loose and rich in nutrients. In spring the trees are still bare, and plenty of light reaches the ground. The spring snowflake uses this time to bloom. It spends the rest of the year as a **bulb** in the soil.

Wild spring snowflakes should be **left standing**. In many Swiss cantons they are protected. Anyone who picks or digs them up harms the populations. In addition, the whole plant is **poisonous**, especially the bulb. If you want them in your garden, buy them from a garden centre.

gewusst: The spring snowflake belongs to the amaryllis family, as do the snowdrop and the daffodil.
Sometimes it is already in bloom when snow still lies in the woods.

teile.einleitung: Plants keep growing at certain places throughout their lives. These places are called meristems. There, cells divide again and again and form new tissue.
wichtigste: A meristem is a plant tissue that can divide and produces new growth.
The apical meristems at the tips of shoots and roots are responsible for growth in length.
The cambium is responsible for the growth of trees in thickness.
Annual rings form because the cambium is active to different degrees during the year.
The root cap protects the meristem at the root tip.
Grasses have meristems at the base of their leaves and grow quickly again after mowing.

abschnitte.text: A **meristem** is a **growth tissue**. Its cells are small, have thin walls and can divide again and again. The new cells later become the different tissues of the plant, for example vessels or leaf cells. These finished tissues are called **permanent tissue**. The word meristem comes from Greek and means roughly “divisible”.

At the tip of every shoot and every root sits an **apical meristem**, also called a **tip meristem**. It makes sure the plant grows **longer**. At the root tip, the meristem pushes its way through the soil. To keep it from being injured, it is protected by a cap of cells, the **root cap**. In grasses there are extra meristems at the **base of the leaves**. That is why they grow back quickly after being mown or grazed.

abschnitte.titel: Growth in thickness and annual rings
abschnitte.text: Trees get a little thicker every year. The **cambium** is responsible for this, a thin layer under the bark. It forms **wood** towards the inside and **bast** towards the outside. In spring light, loose wood forms, and in late summer darker, dense wood. This is how the **annual rings** become visible. Another layer, the **cork cambium**, forms the cork of the **bark** that protects the trunk.

Meristems that are already laid down in the seedling are called **primary meristems**. **Secondary meristems** form later from cells that were already fully developed. These cells become able to divide again. One example is the cork cambium.

In laboratories, whole new plants can be grown from tiny pieces of a tip meristem. This is called **meristem culture**. In this way, for example, **virus-free potato plants** are obtained. Viruses hardly ever reach the meristem, because no vessels have formed there yet.

gewusst: Thanks to their meristems, some trees can live for several thousand years and still keep growing.
You can tell the age of a felled tree from its annual rings.

teile.einleitung: The Moon is a heavenly body that orbits the Earth. It is our nearest neighbour in space and the brightest object in the night sky. To this day it is the only other heavenly body that people have set foot on.
wichtigste: The Moon is the Earth’s natural companion and orbits around it.
On average it is about 384,400 kilometres from the Earth.
Its diameter is about 3,474 kilometres, a good quarter of the Earth’s diameter.
The Moon does not shine by itself, but is lit up by the Sun.
It always shows the same side to the Earth.
In 1969, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin were the first people to set foot on the Moon.
The pull of the Moon causes the tides on Earth.

abschnitte.text: The **Moon** is a satellite, that is a heavenly body that orbits a planet. It is about 384,400 kilometres away; by car you would need more than half a year to get there without a break. For one lap around the Earth it needs about 27 days. Because it turns exactly once on its own axis in that time, we always see the same side. The far side was only photographed in 1959, by a space probe.

Researchers think that about 4.5 billion years ago, a heavenly body the size of Mars collided with the young Earth. The Moon formed from the debris that was thrown out. This heavenly body is called **Theia**. Since then the Moon has been slowly moving away from the Earth, by about 3.8 centimetres a year.

On the Moon there is no air, no liquid water and no weather. The surface is covered with countless **craters** that come from impacts. The dark patches that we see are large plains of solidified lava, called **maria**, which means seas. In the day it gets over 100 degrees hot, at night far below minus 100 degrees cold.

On 20 July 1969, the American mission **Apollo 11** landed on the Moon. Neil Armstrong was the first person to set foot on it. Up to 1972, twelve astronauts in all walked on the surface of the Moon and brought back about 380 kilograms of Moon rock. Because gravity is only about a sixth as strong as on Earth, they could make big jumps.

Switzerland was part of Apollo 11 too. The University of Bern, under Johannes Geiss, developed a **solar wind sail**, a foil that caught particles from the Sun. It was the only non-American experiment of the mission. Buzz Aldrin even put it up in front of the American flag.

The Moon’s gravity pulls on the water of the oceans. This causes **low tide** and **high tide** twice a day. On some coasts the sea rises and falls by several metres. The Moon also stabilises the tilt of the Earth’s axis and so makes for a calmer climate.

begriffe.erklaerung: A heavenly body that orbits a planet, also called a moon.
A bowl-shaped dip made by an impact.
Dark, flat plains of lava on the Moon, once thought to be seas.
The regular rising and falling of sea level, that is low tide and high tide.

gewusst: The astronauts’ footprints can probably still be seen today, because no wind blows on the Moon.
On the Moon, a child who weighs 30 kilograms would feel as light as if they weighed 5 kilograms.
The Moon is about 400 times smaller than the Sun, but also about 400 times closer, so both appear the same size in the sky.

teile.einleitung: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun and is called the “red planet” because of its colour. It is a rocky planet like Earth, but smaller, colder and with very thin air. No other planet has been explored so thoroughly with robots, and one day people may perhaps travel there.
wichtigste: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun.
It is called the “red planet” because of its colour.
The red colour comes from iron oxide, a kind of rust, in the dust and rock.
Mars is about half the size of Earth.
A Martian year lasts 687 Earth days, a Martian day a little over 24 hours.
On Mars stands Olympus Mons, the highest known volcano in the Solar System.
Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos.

abschnitte.text: After Earth, Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun and is one of the **rocky planets**. Its surface is covered with red dust that contains a lot of **iron oxide**, a kind of rust. That is why Mars glows reddish in the night sky and is called the red planet. It is named after the Roman god of war, Mars, because its colour reminded people of blood and fire.

Mars has a diameter of about 6,800 kilometres, which makes it about half the size of Earth. **Gravity** there is only a little over a third as strong: a child who weighs 30 kilograms on Earth would feel like 11 kilograms. A day on Mars, a **sol**, lasts 24 hours and 37 minutes. For one trip around the Sun, Mars needs 687 Earth days, which is almost two Earth years.

Mars has enormous landscapes: the volcano **Olympus Mons** rises more than 20 kilometres high, which is almost three times as high as Mount Everest. The system of canyons called Valles Marineris is about 4,000 kilometres long. The air is mostly carbon dioxide and is so thin that people could not breathe there. On average it is about minus 60 degrees cold, and at the poles there are **polar caps** of water ice and frozen CO2.

Dried-up riverbeds and lake deposits show that liquid **water** flowed on Mars billions of years ago. Today water exists almost only as ice in the ground and at the poles. Researchers are looking for traces of simple life that might once have existed there. So far, however, no sure proof of life on Mars has been found.

Space probes have been flying to Mars since the 1960s, and several **rovers** have driven across its surface. The rover Curiosity landed in 2012, and the rover **Perseverance** in February 2021, together with the little helicopter Ingenuity, which was the first aircraft to fly on another planet. Switzerland takes part in the research too: the University of Bern built the camera **CaSSIS**, which photographs Mars from orbit on board a European probe. Space agencies plan to send people to Mars in the future as well.

begriffe.erklaerung: A planet with a solid surface made of rock, like Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.
A day on Mars. It lasts 24 hours and 37 minutes.
A remote-controlled vehicle that explores the surface of a heavenly body.
A cover of ice around the north or south pole of a planet.

gewusst: On Mars there are sometimes huge dust storms that can wrap the whole planet.
A sunset on Mars looks bluish, which is exactly the opposite of on Earth.
Depending on the distance, a radio signal from Earth takes between about 3 and 22 minutes to reach Mars.

teile.einleitung: A mire (in German a “Moor”) is a permanently wet habitat in which dead plants do not rot completely but slowly pile up into peat. Mires are home to rare plants and animals. They are also important for the climate, because they store large amounts of carbon in the ground.
wichtigste: A mire is a wetland with waterlogged ground in which peat forms.
Peat forms from plant remains that are hardly broken down because of wetness and lack of oxygen.
A distinction is made between raised bogs, which receive only rainwater, and fens, which are fed by groundwater.
Mires store large amounts of carbon in the ground and are therefore important for the climate.
Rare plants such as the carnivorous sundew grow in mires.
In Switzerland, mires have been protected in the constitution since the Rothenthurm initiative of 1987.
A large part of the former Swiss mires has been drained or mined.

abschnitte.text: A **mire** is an area in which the ground is wet all year round. Dead plants sink into the water, where there is hardly any oxygen. That is why they do not rot completely, but form a dark, spongy mass, the **peat**. Peat grows only about a millimetre a year, so a metre of peat takes about a thousand years.

A **raised bog** is supplied with water only by rain and is very poor in nutrients. Here mainly sphagnum moss grows, which slowly curves upwards like a watch glass. A **fen**, also called a low bog, lies by groundwater or on lake shores and is richer in nutrients. There sedges, rushes and orchids grow.

Mires cover only about three per cent of the Earth’s land area, but store about twice as much **carbon** as all the forests put together. If a mire is drained, air gets into the peat. Then it breaks down and releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. That is why it is good for the climate when drained mires are made wet again.

In the nutrient-poor raised bog, plants have developed special tricks. The **sundew** catches small insects with sticky droplets and digests them. The cotton grass stands out with its white, fluffy heads. Dragonflies, moor frogs, adders and rare butterflies also live here.

In the past, many Swiss mires were drained to gain farmland, or peat was mined as fuel. As a result, a large part of the mire areas has been lost since 1800. In 1987 the Swiss voters accepted the **Rothenthurm initiative**, and since then mires and mire landscapes of special beauty have been protected in the Federal Constitution. Well-known mire landscapes lie near Rothenthurm in the canton of Schwyz and in the UNESCO Entlebuch Biosphere.

Because hardly anything rots in a mire, things are preserved for a very long time. Pollen in the peat tells researchers which plants grew thousands of years ago. In Northern Europe, even **bog bodies** have been found, people from the Iron Age whose skin and hair were still preserved. Mires are therefore like a history book of nature.

begriffe.erklaerung: A dark mass of hardly decomposed plant remains that forms in a mire.
A mire that is fed only by rainwater and is very poor in nutrients.
A mire that is fed by groundwater or a body of water.
A habitat with very wet ground, for example a mire, a marsh or a reedbed.

gewusst: Sphagnum moss can store many times its own weight in water, like a sponge.
For a long time, peat was cut in Switzerland as a fuel for heating.
The mire protection initiative was named after the place Rothenthurm, where an army training ground was planned in a mire landscape.

teile.einleitung: Methane is a colourless, odourless gas that burns and is the main component of natural gas. It is produced, among other places, in cows’ stomachs, in swamps and on rice fields. As a greenhouse gas, methane has an especially strong effect on the climate.
wichtigste: Methane is a gas made of one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms; its formula is CH4.
Methane is the main component of natural gas and biogas.
It is a powerful greenhouse gas and contributes to global warming.
Methane is produced, among other ways, by livestock farming, because cows make it in their stomachs and belch it out.
Swamps, rice fields and rubbish tips also release methane.
Methane stays in the atmosphere for only about twelve years, but has a much stronger effect than carbon dioxide.
Mixed with air, methane can explode.

abschnitte.text: **Methane** is the simplest hydrocarbon: one carbon atom is joined to four hydrogen atoms. At room temperature it is a gas that you can neither see nor smell. Because it is lighter than air, it rises. The Italian researcher Alessandro Volta discovered it in 1776 in the marsh gas at Lake Maggiore.

Methane is produced when **bacteria** break down plant remains without oxygen. This happens in the rumen of cows, sheep and goats, in swamps and bogs, on flooded rice fields and in rubbish tips. A cow belches out several hundred litres of methane a day. Methane also escapes when coal, oil and natural gas are extracted. In Switzerland, most of the methane comes from agriculture.

Methane holds back heat in the atmosphere, like carbon dioxide. But it has a much stronger effect: calculated over 20 years, about 80 times as strong as the same amount of **carbon dioxide**. On the other hand, it is broken down again after about twelve years. Since industrialisation began, the amount of methane in the air has more than doubled. Releasing less methane therefore slows warming quickly.

Because methane burns well, it is used as **natural gas** for heating, cooking and generating electricity. So that leaks can be noticed, a substance with a strong smell is added to natural gas. In **biogas plants**, methane is obtained from slurry, manure and green waste. This biogas can also be used as a fuel for cars and buses.

In coal mines, methane sometimes collects, and there it is called firedamp. If it mixes with air, a spark can set off a serious explosion, called a **firedamp explosion**. In the past, miners therefore took canaries with them, which showed signs first when the air was bad. Today, electronic measuring devices give the warning.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gas in the air that holds back heat and warms up the Earth.
A flammable gas from the ground that is mostly methane.
A gas that bacteria produce from manure, slurry or waste.
The largest part of a cow’s stomach, where bacteria break down the grass.

gewusst: On Saturn’s moon Titan there are whole lakes of liquid methane.
Natural gas only smells because a scent is deliberately added to it.
Researchers are testing feed additives so that cows belch out less methane.

teile.einleitung: A mixed forest is a forest of broadleaved and coniferous trees growing side by side. Because many different tree species occur here, an especially large number of animals and plants find a home too. In Switzerland, mixed forests are very common.
wichtigste: A mixed forest is made up of broadleaved and coniferous trees.
Typical trees in Swiss mixed forests are beech, silver fir, spruce, maple and ash.
The forest is divided into layers: moss layer, herb layer, shrub layer and tree layer.
Mixed forests are more resilient than pure spruce forests, because pests and storms do not hit all the trees equally.
The hurricane Lothar destroyed large areas of forest in Switzerland on 26 December 1999.
In the Emmental there are selection forests, in which trees of all ages stand side by side.
Because of climate change, foresters now increasingly rely on mixed forests.

abschnitte.text: A **mixed forest** is a forest in which broadleaved and coniferous trees grow together. In Switzerland these are often beeches, silver firs and spruces, together with maple, ash, oak or cherry. In autumn the broadleaved trees turn colourful, while most conifers stay green. In the Swiss Central Plateau, without people, mostly beech forest and mixed beech and fir forest would grow.

A forest is built like a house with floors, which is called **layering**. At the very bottom lies the moss layer with mosses, fungi and leaf litter. Above it comes the **herb layer** with ferns, grasses and flowers such as the wood anemone. Then comes the shrub layer with elder or hazel, and at the very top the tree layer with the crowns of the big trees.

Because a mixed forest has many tree species and layers, it is especially rich in species. Woodpeckers hammer holes into old trees, squirrels collect beechnuts and fir seeds. Roe deer, foxes, badgers and many beetles live here. Deadwood, that is dead trees, is an important habitat for fungi and insects. It is said that the forest has a high **biodiversity**.

On 26 December 1999, the hurricane **Lothar** swept across Switzerland. On the Uetliberg, gusts of 241 kilometres per hour were measured. About 10 million trees were blown down, especially many spruces in pure spruce forests. After the storm, the bark beetle also multiplied strongly. This experience showed that mixed forests cope better with storms and pests.

In a **selection forest**, young, middle-aged and old trees of all sizes stand in a colourful mix side by side. The forester only ever fells individual trees, instead of clearing whole areas. In this way the forest stays permanently closed and protects the soil. In the Emmental and in other Pre-Alpine areas, this kind of forest management with silver fir, spruce and beech has a long tradition.

Because of climate change it is getting warmer and drier. The spruce suffers especially from heat and drought. That is why foresters increasingly plant tree species that cope better with warmth, such as oak, Douglas fir or silver fir. A well-mixed forest spreads the **risk**: if one species fails, others stay standing.

begriffe.erklaerung: The division of the forest into layers from the ground up to the tree crowns.
The forest layer of grasses, ferns and flowers directly above the moss layer.
A forest in which trees of all ages stand mixed side by side.
A small beetle that lives under the bark and attacks weakened spruces.

gewusst: About a third of the area of Switzerland is covered by forest.
In Switzerland, Lothar blew down in a single day about as much timber as is otherwise harvested in two to three years.
Switzerland has had a law protecting the forest since 1876.

teile.einleitung: Mars has two small moons, called Phobos and Deimos. They are not round like our Moon, but look like irregular, potato-shaped lumps of rock full of craters. They were only discovered in 1877, because they are so small and dark.
wichtigste: The two moons of Mars are called Phobos and Deimos.
Both moons were discovered in 1877 by the American astronomer Asaph Hall.
Phobos means fear, Deimos means terror.
The moons are small and irregularly shaped like potatoes.
Phobos is bigger and orbits much closer to Mars than Deimos.
Phobos is slowly approaching Mars and will break apart or crash in many millions of years.
The moons may be captured asteroids or debris from an impact.

abschnitte.text: Mars has exactly two natural **moons**: Phobos and Deimos. They are among the smallest moons in the Solar System. Phobos is about 27 kilometres long, Deimos only about 15 kilometres, so both would fit comfortably inside a small Swiss canton. Both are very dark and have a surface covered in **craters**.

In August 1877, the American astronomer **Asaph Hall** discovered the two moons with a large telescope in Washington. He named them after the sons of the Greek god of war Ares, who was called Mars by the Romans. **Phobos** means fear and **Deimos** means terror. In legend, the two accompanied their father into battle.

Phobos orbits at a height of only about 6,000 kilometres above the surface of Mars and needs less than 8 hours for one lap. Because it orbits faster than Mars turns, it rises in the west and sets in the east, and does so twice a day. Deimos is further away and needs about 30 hours for one orbit. Phobos gets about two centimetres closer to Mars every year and, in many millions of years, will be torn apart by **tidal forces** or crash onto Mars.

On Phobos the huge crater **Stickney** stands out. It is about 9 kilometres across, a third of the length of the whole moon. The impact that made it almost broke Phobos apart. Long grooves also run across the surface of Phobos. Deimos looks smoother, because many craters are filled with fine **dust**.

How the moons of Mars were formed is still not clearly settled. One idea is that they are **asteroids** that Mars captured with its gravity. Another idea is that they formed from debris that a huge **impact** on Mars flung into space. The Japanese mission MMX is meant to bring soil samples from Phobos to Earth and help settle this question.

begriffe.erklaerung: A heavenly body that orbits a planet.
A bowl-shaped dip, usually made by the impact of a lump of rock.
Forces that arise from the different pull of a heavenly body and that can deform other bodies.
A small body of rock that orbits the Sun.

gewusst: The writer Jonathan Swift wrote about two moons of Mars as early as 1726 in his book about Gulliver’s travels, over 150 years before their discovery.
On Phobos gravity is so weak that a strong jump would carry a person very far up.
Seen from Mars, Deimos looks hardly bigger in the sky than a bright star.

teile.einleitung: A meteoroid is a small lump of rock or metal that flies through space. If it hits the Earth, it usually burns up as a glowing shooting star. Only rarely does a remnant survive and land on the ground as a meteorite.
wichtigste: A meteoroid is a small body of rock or metal that orbits the Sun.
Meteoroids are smaller than asteroids, and many are only as big as a grain of sand.
The meteoroid is the body in space, the meteor is its glow as it enters the atmosphere.
A meteorite is the remnant that reaches the ground.
In everyday speech, meteors are also called shooting stars.
Many meteoroids come from comets or from broken-up asteroids.
In meteor showers such as the Perseids in August, you see especially many shooting stars.

abschnitte.text: A **meteoroid** is a small lump of rock or metal that flies through our Solar System. Most are tiny, only a few millimetres across. Bigger lumps of many metres are usually called asteroids. Meteoroids orbit the Sun like the planets, but on very different paths.

These three words sound similar, but mean different things. The **meteoroid** is the body in space. When it races into the Earth’s envelope of air, the air in front of it is squeezed and heated so strongly that it glows: this glow is called a **meteor**. What is left of it and reaches the ground is called a **meteorite**.

Meteoroids hit the Earth’s atmosphere at 11 to over 70 kilometres per second. That is much faster than a rifle bullet. They begin to glow at a height of about 80 to 120 kilometres. Most burn up completely before they get lower than 50 kilometres. Especially bright meteors are called **fireballs** or bolides.

Comets lose dust and small stones along their path. If the Earth crosses this trail of dust every year, a **meteor shower** results. The Perseids in August come from the comet Swift-Tuttle. In December you can watch the Geminids. On dark nights you then sometimes see dozens of shooting stars per hour.

Meteorites are roughly divided into stony meteorites, iron meteorites and stony-iron meteorites. The biggest known meteorite is the Hoba meteorite in Namibia, which weighs about 60 tonnes. In Switzerland, many pieces of an iron meteorite have been found at the **Twannberg** in the canton of Bern. Meteorites are valuable for research because they show what the young Solar System was made of.

Very big lumps can leave craters. In 2013, an object about 20 metres across exploded over the Russian city of Chelyabinsk, and the shock wave broke many window panes. About 66 million years ago, a huge asteroid hit Mexico and helped to wipe out the dinosaurs. But events like this are extremely rare.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small lump of rock or metal flying through space.
The streak of light in the sky when a meteoroid burns up in the air.
A piece from space that has fallen all the way to the ground.
Many shooting stars that come at the same time of year from the same direction of the sky.

gewusst: Every day, tonnes of tiny grains of dust fall from space onto the Earth.
Most shooting stars are made by grains smaller than a grain of rice.
Some meteorites come from Mars or from the Moon.

teile.einleitung: Table, chair, bed and shelf: in every home there is **furniture**. A lot of it is made of **wood**, a raw material from the forest. Wood is sturdy, warm and easy to work.
wichtigste: A chair has a seat and a back.
A table usually has four legs and a top.
Anyone who builds furniture from wood is a joiner.
Pieces of wood are joined firmly with screws and glue.
Oil, wax or varnish protect wooden furniture and make it shine.
Books stand on the shelf; clothes and things lie in the drawers of a chest of drawers.

abschnitte.text: For sitting there is the **chair** with a seat and a back. At the **table**, with its top and usually four legs, we eat, play and learn. For sleeping we need a **bed**. Books are usually kept on the **shelf**. A **chest of drawers** has drawers in which you can put clothes or toys.

Different kinds of wood are used for furniture. **Spruce** and **fir** are pale and rather soft. **Beech** and **oak** are hard and very sturdy. **Walnut** has a beautiful, dark pattern. In Switzerland a lot of wood grows, and it is also used for furniture. Wood is a **renewable raw material**, because new trees keep growing in the forest.

Anyone who builds furniture from wood is a **joiner**, called a **“Schreiner”** in Swiss German. In Germany a joiner is also called a “Tischler”. In the workshop stands a **workbench**, a sturdy work table. There wood is sawn, planed and sanded. The pieces of wood are joined with **screws and glue**, and sometimes with wooden dowels. Today machines that cut very precisely help with this too.

Untreated wood soon gets stained and soaks up water. That is why furniture is protected with **oil, wax or varnish**. Oil and wax sink into the wood and bring out the grain beautifully. Varnish forms a hard layer on the surface. In this way wooden furniture stays beautiful for many years and can even be handed down.

gewusst: The lines in wood are called the grain. They come from the tree’s annual rings.
Good wooden furniture can be repaired and sanded down again if it is scratched.

teile.einleitung: The weather is not the same everywhere, even when places lie close together. In a hollow, on the wall of a house or in a wood, there is often a climate all of its own. This is called a microclimate.
wichtigste: A microclimate is the climate in a small space, such as a garden, a wood or a street.
On clear nights, cold air collects in hollows, where there is often ground frost.
A large lake smooths out temperature swings on its shore.
In a wood it is cooler and damper on summer days than in an open field.
Between tall buildings the wind is speeded up: the funnel effect.
Weather stations usually measure the air temperature 2 metres above the ground.

abschnitte.text: The **microclimate** describes temperature, humidity, wind and sun in a small space. It depends on how the ground is shaped, what grows on it and which buildings stand there. A south-facing slope is warmer than a north-facing one. A dark asphalt square heats up more than a meadow. So that measurements can be compared, **weather stations** usually measure the air temperature **2 metres** above the ground.

Cold air is heavier than warm air. On clear, still nights the ground cools strongly, and the cold air flows downhill like water. In **hollows** and **depressions** it collects into a **cold-air pool**. There you often get **ground frost**, while it stays milder on the slope above. A well-known example is the high valley of **La Brévine** in the Jura, which is called the “Siberia of Switzerland”.

Water warms up slowly and cools down slowly. A large **lake** therefore makes the climate on its shore more even. In **Lavaux** on Lake Geneva, vines grow on steep terraces. It is said that **three suns** work there: the sun in the sky, its light reflected from the **lake**, and the warmth of the **walls**. Lavaux has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007.

In a **wood**, the tree crowns give shade, and the leaves give off water. That is why it is **cooler and damper** there on summer days than in a field. In the garden, people use the microclimate on purpose. Fruit trees are often trained as **espaliers** on a **south-facing wall**. The wall stores heat in the day and gives it off again at night, so the fruit ripens better.

Cities are often warmer than the land around them, because concrete and asphalt store a lot of heat. This is called a **heat island**. Between tall buildings the wind is squeezed together and so gets faster. This is called the **funnel effect**. Trees, parks and fountains help to cool the city on hot days.

gewusst: On the Glattalp in the canton of Schwyz, in a hollow full of cold air, about minus 52 degrees was measured in the winter of 1991.
The difference between a sunny south-facing slope and a shady north-facing slope can decide the plant life of a whole valley.

teile.einleitung: Meteorology is the science of the weather and of the Earth’s envelope of air. Meteorologists measure temperature, wind and rain and predict what the weather will be like in the coming days. Without them we would not know whether we need an umbrella tomorrow.
wichtigste: Meteorology is the study of the weather and of the processes in the atmosphere.
A meteorologist forecasts the weather on television, for example.
Among other things, temperature, air pressure, humidity, wind and precipitation are measured.
Weather forecasts are calculated today with high-performance computers.
In Switzerland, the federal office MeteoSwiss is responsible for weather and climate.
The further into the future a forecast reaches, the less certain it becomes.
Meteorology also warns of dangers such as storms, thunderstorms or heat.

abschnitte.text: **Meteorology** investigates what happens in the Earth’s envelope of air. The word comes from Greek and means roughly “the study of things in the air”. Over 2,300 years ago, the Greek scholar Aristotle already wrote a book about clouds, rain and wind. Meteorology deals with the weather of today and tomorrow, **climatology** with the weather over many decades.

For a good forecast you need many measurements. A thermometer measures the temperature, a **barometer** the air pressure, a hygrometer the humidity and an anemometer the wind speed. Weather balloons rise to over 30 kilometres and take measurements on the way. Weather satellites photograph the clouds from space, and weather radars detect rain and hail.

All the measurements from around the world are fed into **weather models**. These are computer programs that use the laws of physics to calculate how air, heat and moisture move. This takes extremely fast supercomputers. Then experts look at the results and write the forecast from them. For the next two to three days, forecasts are usually quite reliable today.

In Switzerland, **MeteoSwiss**, the Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology, is responsible for weather and climate. It runs a dense network of automatic measuring stations and five weather radars, including on the Albis and on Monte Lema. In Payerne, weather balloons are released every day. The weather station on the Säntis has been taking measurements since 1882.

Meteorologists warn of severe weather such as thunderstorms, hail, storms, heavy rain or heatwaves. In Switzerland the warnings have five levels. Aircraft, ships, farming and ski resorts also need accurate weather data. In the mountains, the **avalanche warning** is closely tied to the weather forecast.

begriffe.erklaerung: A prediction of what the weather will be like in the future.
An instrument for measuring air pressure.
A computer program that calculates how the weather will develop.
A warm, dry wind that blows down the slopes into Alpine valleys.

gewusst: A weather balloon gets bigger and bigger at great height until it bursts.
The weather station on the Säntis has been taking measurements for over 140 years.
The barometer was invented in 1643 by the Italian Evangelista Torricelli.

teile.einleitung: A monsoon forest is a tropical forest with a rainy season and a dry season. In the rainy season it is dense and green, in the dry season many trees stand bare. It is especially widespread in South and Southeast Asia.
wichtigste: In a monsoon forest, the rainy season and the dry season take turns.
Many trees drop their leaves in the dry season to save water.
It is also called a rain-green forest.
The teak tree is a typical tree of monsoon forests.
The tiger lives in the monsoon forests of India.
The word “monsoon” comes from Arabic.

abschnitte.text: The **monsoon** is a wind over a large area that changes its direction over the course of the year. In summer it brings damp air from the sea and heavy rainfall. In winter it blows from the land and is dry. The word comes from **Arabic** and means roughly “season”. The monsoon shapes the lives of hundreds of millions of people.

In the **rainy season**, the trees put out new leaves, and the forest is lushly green. In the **dry season**, many trees drop their leaves. In this way they lose less water through their leaves. Because the forest has leaves mainly in the rainy season, it is also called a **rain-green forest**. It is lighter and less rich in species than the always-damp rainforest.

Monsoon forests are especially widespread in **South and Southeast Asia**, for example in India, Myanmar and Thailand. Similar forests with a rainy and a dry season are also found in parts of Africa, South America and northern Australia. Many monsoon forests have been cleared to make room for fields, plantations and settlements.

A typical tree of the monsoon forests is the **teak tree**. Its wood is hard, heavy and very resistant to water and pests. That is why **teak** is used for ships, garden furniture and floors. Because teak wood is so sought after, it is now often grown on plantations.

In the monsoon forests of **India** lives the **tiger**, the biggest cat in the world. Asian elephants, leopards, deer and many species of monkey are also at home there. The animals have to adapt to the change of seasons. In the dry season they often gather at waterholes.

gewusst: In some areas of India, almost the whole year’s rain falls in a few months of the monsoon.
Teak wood contains natural oils that protect it from rot.

teile.einleitung: A monoculture is the growing of only a single plant species over a large area, often for many years. In this way huge amounts of maize, wheat or palm oil can be harvested efficiently. But monocultures also have big disadvantages for soil, animals and plants.
wichtigste: A monoculture is the growing of a single plant species over a large area.
Examples are huge fields of maize or soya, oil palm plantations and pure spruce forests.
Monocultures can be worked and harvested easily with machines.
Pests and diseases can spread very quickly in monocultures.
The soil loses nutrients when it is always used in the same way.
Monocultures offer a home to only a few animals and plants.
Crop rotation and companion planting are alternatives to monoculture.

abschnitte.text: The word **monoculture** is put together from the Greek “mono” for alone and “culture” for growing. It means that only a single plant species grows in a field or a forest. Often the same plant is even grown in the same place year after year. In the USA there are maize fields that reach to the horizon.

Monocultures are easy to farm. All the plants are sown, fertilised and harvested at the same time, so large **machines** can be used. In this way a lot of food can be produced with little work. A uniform harvest is also convenient for trade.

In a monoculture, **pests** and disease-causing organisms find plenty of food and spread rapidly. That is why a lot of pesticides are often needed. The soil is drained of nutrients in a one-sided way, and without a protective plant cover, rain and wind can carry the soil away, which is called **erosion**. There is also little habitat for insects, birds and wild plants.

Between 1845 and 1849, a fungal disease, **potato blight**, destroyed almost the whole potato harvest in Ireland. Because many people lived almost only on potatoes, a severe famine followed. Bananas have this problem too: the once popular variety Gros Michel was almost wiped out by a fungal disease in the 20th century. Today the Cavendish variety is also under threat.

For palm oil, huge areas of rainforest were cleared in Indonesia and Malaysia and replaced by **plantations**. In Brazil, soya beans grow over vast areas, mainly as animal feed. As a result, orangutans and many other species lose their habitat. Pure spruce forests are also monocultures and suffer badly from storms and bark beetles.

In **crop rotation**, the plant species in a field is changed every year, for example wheat, then potatoes, then clover. In companion planting, several species grow side by side at the same time. In Switzerland, farms that receive direct payments have to follow a regulated crop rotation. The rather small fields make the Swiss landscape more varied than many farming landscapes abroad.

begriffe.erklaerung: Growing only one plant species over a large area.
The yearly change of the plants grown in a field.
The wearing away of soil by wind and water.
A large farm on which usually only one crop grows.

gewusst: Almost all the bananas in the supermarket belong to the same variety and are nearly identical genetically.
Because of the famine in Ireland, over a million people emigrated, many to America.
Even a perfect English lawn is really a small monoculture.

teile.einleitung: When leaves, roots and dead animals rot in the soil, they do not simply disappear. Tiny living things break them down into simple substances. In soil science, this process is called mineralisation.
wichtigste: Mineralisation is the breakdown of organic matter into inorganic compounds.
Bacteria and fungi in the soil do this work.
In the process, nutrients become available to plants again.
In mineralisation with oxygen, the carbon escapes as carbon dioxide.
It runs fastest in warm, damp, well-aerated soil.
In waterlogged raised bogs it is held back, which is why peat forms there.

abschnitte.text: Organic matter is material that comes from living things, such as dead leaves or roots. In **mineralisation**, **micro-organisms** such as bacteria and fungi break these remains down. What is left is simple **inorganic compounds**: carbon dioxide, water, ammonium, nitrate, phosphate and other minerals. Earthworms and woodlice help by first chopping up the remains.

Plants are the **producers** in an ecosystem. They take up nutrients from the soil and build their bodies from them. When they die, mineralisation makes sure these nutrients become **available again**. Without this breakdown, the nutrients would stay locked in dead remains. The living things that do the breaking down are called **decomposers**.

When mineralisation runs with oxygen, it is called **aerobic**. The carbon from the remains then gets into the air as **carbon dioxide**. How active the micro-organisms are is therefore measured by the amount of carbon dioxide a soil gives off. This measurement is called **soil respiration**. A living soil “breathes” strongly.

Micro-organisms work best when it is **warm**, **damp** and **well aerated**. In cold, dry or very wet soils, the breakdown is slow. In **raised bogs** the ground is permanently wet, and there is no oxygen. That is why plant remains are hardly broken down there and pile up into thick **layers of peat**.

Not all remains are broken down completely. Part of them is turned into stable **humic substances**, which form the dark **humus**. This process is called **humification**. If a farmer works a lot of **straw** into the soil, it contains a lot of carbon but little nitrogen. It is said to have a **wide C/N ratio**. The micro-organisms then take nitrogen from the soil for a while, so it is missing for the plants.

gewusst: In a handful of soil live more micro-organisms than there are people on Earth.
In the peat of bogs, you sometimes find plant remains that are thousands of years old.

teile.einleitung: Macroinvertebrates, known in science as macrozoobenthos, are the small invertebrate animals on the bed of streams, rivers and lakes that can still be seen with the naked eye. They tell us a lot about how clean a body of water is.
wichtigste: They include insect larvae, snails, mussels, worms and small crustaceans.
Mayflies, stoneflies and caddisflies make up the EPT taxa.
Many of their larvae need clean, oxygen-rich water.
Caddisfly larvae build a case out of small stones or plant parts.
The Swiss index IBCH assesses bodies of water using these animals.
The freshwater shrimp is a crustacean and chops up fallen leaves.

abschnitte.text: The word is put together from Greek: **makro** means large, **zoon** animal and **benthos** bed. It means invertebrate animals that you can see without a microscope and that live on and in the **bed of a body of water**. They include **insect larvae**, snails, mussels, worms and **small crustaceans**. You find them under stones, in sand and among water plants.

Three groups of insects are seen as indicators of good water quality: **mayflies**, **stoneflies** and **caddisflies**. Their scientific names Ephemeroptera, Plecoptera and Trichoptera give the abbreviation **EPT**. Many of their larvae need clean, oxygen-rich water. Stonefly larvae have **two** tail filaments, while most mayfly larvae have three. Caddisfly larvae glue sand, small stones or plant parts together with silk to make a **case** that protects their soft abdomen.

The animals feed in different ways. The **shredders** eat leaves that have fallen into the water. They include the **freshwater shrimp** Gammarus and some caddisfly larvae. The freshwater shrimp is a **crustacean** and, despite its name, is not related to fleas. Shredders make the energy in the leaves of the trees along the bank available to the whole body of water.

Many animals that live on the bed let go of it and drift downstream with the current. This drifting with the water is called **drift**. It happens mostly **at night**, when fish find it harder to see the animals. In this way the animals spread out through the body of water.

In Switzerland there is the index **IBCH**, the **Indice Biologique Suisse**. It is part of the federal government’s **modular stepwise procedure** for investigating bodies of water. Experts work out which **families** of invertebrates living on the bed are present in a sample. From this they calculate how good the condition of the water is.

gewusst: Some mayflies live as adult insects for only a few hours to days, but as larvae they live in the water for much longer.
The larvae often spend most of their lives in the stream.
