teile.einleitung: In almost every cell of plants, animals and fungi there are tiny parts that provide energy. They are called mitochondria. They are often called the power stations of the cell.
wichtigste: Mitochondria gain energy through cellular respiration.
In the process they use up oxygen.
They make the energy carrier ATP.
Carbon dioxide and water are produced as waste.
A mitochondrion is surrounded by two membranes; the inner one forms folds, the cristae.
Plant cells have mitochondria too, not only animal cells.

abschnitte.text: Every cell needs energy to grow, to move or to make substances. This energy is gained by the **mitochondria**. That is why they are often called the **power stations of the cell**. A single mitochondrion is so small that you can only see it under the microscope. A cell can contain many hundreds of them.

**Cellular respiration** takes place in the mitochondria. Sugar is broken down with **oxygen**. The energy that is released is stored by the cell in the molecule **ATP**. ATP is like a small battery that can be used anywhere in the cell. **Carbon dioxide** and **water** are produced as waste. We breathe the carbon dioxide out again with the air.

A mitochondrion is surrounded by **two membranes**. The outer one is smooth. The inner one is strongly folded; these folds are called **cristae**. The folds make the surface bigger, and there is more room for the parts that make ATP. The space inside is called the **matrix**.

Many people think plants do not need mitochondria because they carry out photosynthesis. But **plant cells** have mitochondria **just like animal cells**. In the **chloroplasts**, plants use light to make sugar. In the mitochondria they break this sugar down again to gain energy. They do this day and night.

Mitochondria have a small **genetic material** of their own, like bacteria. Researchers assume that a very long time ago they arose from bacteria that were taken into another cell. This explanation is called the **endosymbiotic theory**. Today it is seen as well supported.

gewusst: Muscle cells and heart cells contain especially many mitochondria, because they need a lot of energy.
Human red blood cells have no mitochondria.

teile.einleitung: A plant grows only as well as the scarcest nutrient allows. This rule is called the law of the minimum. It is important for farming and for understanding lakes and other ecosystems.
wichtigste: The law of the minimum says: the factor that is most lacking limits growth.
Carl Sprengel formulated it as early as 1828.
Justus von Liebig made it well known in the 19th century.
In the minimum barrel, the shortest stave stands for the limiting factor.
Besides nutrients, light, water and temperature can also be at the minimum.
In many Swiss lakes, phosphorus is the minimum factor for the growth of algae.

abschnitte.text: The agricultural scientist **Carl Sprengel** described the law of the minimum as early as **1828**. But it became well known through the chemist **Justus von Liebig**, who wrote a great deal about plant nutrition and fertiliser in the 19th century. That is why people often speak of **Liebig’s law of the minimum**. Today it is sometimes also called the law of Sprengel and Liebig.

The **minimum barrel** is used to illustrate it. A wooden barrel is made of many boards, the **staves**. Each stave stands for a growth factor. If the staves are of different lengths, the water spills over at the **shortest** one. In the same way, the scarcest factor limits how high the yield will be. A longer stave elsewhere is no use.

If a soil lacks **phosphorus** but has enough nitrogen, extra **nitrogen fertiliser** hardly brings any **extra yield**. First the missing phosphorus must be added. The researcher **Eilhard Alfred Mitscherlich** also showed that every further dose of fertiliser brings a smaller and smaller **extra yield**. For farming this means: fertilise in a targeted way and in moderation.

**Light**, **water** and **temperature** can also be at the minimum. In a desert, water usually limits growth; in a dark wood, it is often light. Victor **Shelford’s** **law of tolerance** extends the law of the minimum: not only a lack but also **too much** of a factor can limit growth, for example too much heat or too much water.

In many lakes, **phosphorus** is the factor that limits the **growth of algae**. In the 20th century, when a lot of phosphorus from waste water and agriculture got into Swiss lakes, algae grew in huge numbers there. When the algae were broken down, oxygen ran short. With sewage treatment plants and the ban on phosphate in detergents in 1986, the amount of phosphorus was greatly reduced, and many lakes recovered.

gewusst: The law of the minimum applies in cooking too: if one ingredient is missing, it is no use taking more of another.
When you fix the minimum factor, another factor often becomes the new minimum.

teile.einleitung: On almost every farm there is a manure heap. What smells like rubbish is very valuable for farming. Manure is a natural fertiliser for fields and gardens.
wichtigste: Manure is made of animal dung, urine and straw from the stable.
Farmers use manure to fertilise their fields.
A manure heap is warm inside, so it steams on cold days.
By hand, manure is loaded with a pitchfork.
Fresh manure is not put directly on young plants, because it is too harsh.
The scarab beetle is a beetle that shapes balls out of dung.

abschnitte.text: In the stable, **straw** lies as bedding. It soaks up the animals’ **dung** and urine. This mixture is called **manure** or **solid manure**. The liquid mixture of dung, urine and water, on the other hand, is called **slurry**. Both together are called **farmyard manure**, because they are produced right on the farm. In Switzerland the manure heap is also called a **“Miststock”**.

Manure contains important **nutrients** such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Farmers spread it on the fields with a **manure spreader**. There it is broken down by living things in the soil, and the plants take up the nutrients. Manure also improves the **humus** in the soil. By hand, manure is loaded onto the wheelbarrow with a **pitchfork**.

Inside a manure heap, countless **micro-organisms** are at work. They break down the manure and produce **heat** in the process. That is why a manure heap is warm inside. On cold days you can see **steam** rising. In the past this heat was used for **hotbeds**: under the soil of a cold frame lay fresh horse manure, which warmed the ground.

**Fresh manure** is **too harsh** for young plants. It can damage their delicate roots. That is why it is first left to stand for a few months, until it has rotted well. Gardeners like to use **horse manure**, for example for **roses**. It is loose and warms up quickly. Manure from cows, sheep or hens is also used.

A manure heap is a habitat for many animals. In summer, **flies** often buzz around it and lay their eggs there. Worms and beetles live in the manure. The **scarab beetle** shapes balls out of dung and rolls them away. Its larvae grow up inside them. In ancient Egypt this beetle was sacred as the **scarab**.

gewusst: The heat in a large manure heap can get so high that you would hardly want to leave your hand in it.
On pastures, dung beetles help to get the animals’ dung quickly into the soil.

teile.einleitung: To grow, plants need not only light, water and carbon dioxide, but also nutrients from the soil. Some of these they need only in tiny amounts. These are called micronutrients or trace elements.
wichtigste: Plants need micronutrients only in very small amounts, macronutrients in large amounts.
Micronutrients include iron, manganese, zinc, copper, boron, molybdenum, nickel and chlorine.
Molybdenum is a component of the enzyme nitrogenase.
Manganese takes part in the splitting of water in photosynthesis.
If a micronutrient is missing, the plant shows typical symptoms of deficiency.
Too much of a micronutrient can be poisonous.

abschnitte.text: Plant nutrients are divided up by the **amount needed**. **Macronutrients** such as nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulphur are needed by the plant in plenty. **Micronutrients** it needs only in traces, which is why they are also called **trace elements**. They are indispensable all the same. If just one is missing, the plant cannot grow properly.

Many micronutrients sit in **enzymes**, which are proteins that speed up chemical processes in the cell. **Molybdenum** is found in **nitrogenase**, with which nodule bacteria fix nitrogen from the air. **Nickel** is needed by the enzyme **urease**, which splits urea. **Copper** is contained in the protein **plastocyanin**, which carries electrons in photosynthesis.

In photosynthesis, water is split, and oxygen is produced. **Manganese** takes part in this **splitting of water** in **photosystem II**. The plant needs **iron** to make chlorophyll. If iron is missing, young leaves turn yellow while the leaf veins stay green. This yellowing is called **chlorosis**. It often occurs on soils rich in lime.

In **sugar beet**, a **lack of boron** leads to **heart rot and dry rot**: the inner leaves die, and the beet goes rotten. A **lack of zinc** shows in fruit trees as **small leaves** standing in rosette-like tufts. Farmers can tell from signs like these what the soil is missing. Then they can fertilise in a targeted way.

With micronutrients, too little and too much often lie close together. Too much copper or boron can damage the plant. That is why trace elements are only applied when there is really a deficiency. The soil plays a part as well: if it is very rich in lime or very acid, the plant may take up some substances poorly even though they are there.

gewusst: Humans also need trace elements such as iron, zinc and iodine, but only in tiny amounts.
Without the enzyme nitrogenase and its molybdenum, beans and clover could not use nitrogen from the air.

teile.einleitung: If you climb a mountain in Switzerland, you pass through different altitude zones, each with its own climate and plants. The montane zone is the zone of mountain forests and mountain meadows. It shapes large parts of the Pre-Alps and the Jura.
wichtigste: The term “montane” comes from the Latin word for mountain.
On the northern side of the Alps the montane zone lies roughly between 600 and 1,200 or 1,400 metres.
Typical are forests of beech and silver fir, with spruce added further up.
The climate is cooler and wetter than on the Central Plateau.
Dairy farming on meadows and pastures is typical.
In the Jura there are wooded pastures, where trees stand scattered loosely.

abschnitte.text: It gets cooler as you go higher. That is why mountains are divided into **altitude zones**. At the very bottom lies the **colline zone**, and above it follows the **montane zone**. Higher up come the **subalpine**, the **alpine** and the **nival zone**. The name “montane” comes from the Latin word **mons**, which means “mountain”. On the northern side of the Alps the montane zone reaches roughly from **600 to 1,200 or 1,400 metres**.

Many natural forests of the montane zone are made up of **beech** and **silver fir**. They are called **beech and fir forests**. In the upper montane zone, **spruce** is often added. Still further up, in the subalpine zone, spruce becomes the most important tree. Today many forests have been changed by forestry, and there are often more spruces than would be natural.

In the montane zone it is **cooler** and **wetter** than on the Central Plateau. Snow stays on the ground longer in winter, and the growing season for plants is shorter. It is often too cool and too steep for arable farming. But grass grows well, because there is enough rain.

Typical of the montane zone are **meadows and pastures** with **dairy farming**. The cows graze in summer, and the grass of the meadows is made into hay for the winter. In many places, cheese is made from the milk. Landscapes such as the Emmental or the Toggenburg lie largely in this zone. In the **Pre-Alps** and in the **Jura** it takes up most of the slopes.

abschnitte.titel: The wooded pastures of the Jura
abschnitte.text: In the **Jura** there is a special landscape: the **wooded pastures**, called **“Wytweiden”** in German. On these pastures, single trees or small groups of trees stand scattered loosely, often mighty spruces. The areas are used as pasture and as forest at the same time. The animals find food and, in the shade of the trees, shelter. Wooded pastures are varied habitats.

gewusst: On the southern side of the Alps the altitude zones lie somewhat higher than on the northern side, because it is warmer there.
The limits of the altitude zones are not sharp lines, but merge gradually into one another.

teile.einleitung: Flour is found in bread, cakes, pasta and many sauces. It is made when grains of cereal are finely ground. Depending on which parts of the grain stay in the flour, it is light or dark.
wichtigste: Flour is made from ground cereal grains, for example wheat, spelt or rye.
White flour is light because the dark husk of the grain has been removed.
In Switzerland people distinguish between white flour, half-white flour, Ruch flour and wholemeal flour.
Ruch bread is baked from the dark Ruch flour.
Flour is mostly starch, which gives the body energy.
Flour is stored dry and well sealed.

abschnitte.text: A grain of cereal has three important parts: the **husk**, the small **germ** and the pale **endosperm** inside. In the **mill** the grain is crushed between rollers or stones and then sieved. The separated parts of the husk are called **bran**. In the past a water wheel often drove the millstones. Today big mills work with machines and very fine sieves.

For **white flour**, almost only the pale endosperm is used. **Half-white flour** contains a little more of the grain and is therefore medium-light. **Ruch flour** still has more of the husk in it, so it is darker and tastes stronger. For **wholemeal flour**, the whole grain is ground. Dark flours contain more **dietary fibre** and minerals than white flour.

The most important part of flour is **starch**. It gives the body energy. Added to this are protein, a little fat, water and minerals. In wheat and spelt flour there is a special protein, the **gluten**. It makes the dough stretchy, so that bread can rise nicely.

From flour, eggs and milk you stir a runny batter for **omelettes**, which are fried thin in the frying pan. With water, salt and yeast it becomes bread dough. If you stir a little flour into a sauce, it becomes **thicker** as it cooks. The starch takes up water and swells. This is called **thickening** the sauce.

Flour belongs in a **dry**, cool place and in a well-sealed container. If it gets damp, it can go **mouldy**. Small animals like to settle in old, open stores. A well-known example is the **mealworm**: it is the larva of the mealworm beetle and eats flour and grain.

gewusst: Fine flour dust in the air can catch fire and explode. That is why strict safety rules apply in mills.
Mealworms are bred and sold as food for birds and reptiles.

teile.einleitung: The phases of the Moon are the different shapes that the Moon shows in the sky over the course of a month. Sometimes it is a thin crescent, sometimes half, sometimes perfectly round. The Moon itself does not change, only the part that we see lit up.
wichtigste: Over the course of a month the Moon shows different phases.
The four main phases are called new moon, first quarter, full moon and last quarter.
A complete cycle from one new moon to the next takes about 29.5 days.
The Sun always lights up one half of the Moon.
Depending on the positions of the Sun, Earth and Moon, we see more or less of this bright half.
The phases of the Moon are not caused by the Earth’s shadow.
The word “month” comes from the word “moon”.

abschnitte.titel: What are the phases of the Moon?
abschnitte.text: The Moon does not shine by itself, but is lit up by the Sun. Exactly one half of the Moon is always bright. As the Moon orbits the Earth, we look at this bright half from different angles. So we see sometimes a lot of it, sometimes a little: these are the **phases of the Moon**.

At **new moon**, the Moon stands between the Earth and the Sun, the lit side faces away from us, and we cannot see it. After that a thin crescent becomes visible, and the Moon is **waxing**. After about a week it is half lit, which is the first quarter. After about two weeks we see the whole bright side, and it is **full moon**. After that it wanes again, until it is new moon once more.

Here in the Northern Hemisphere, the right side is bright when the Moon is waxing. When the Moon is waning, the left side shines. An old German memory aid: if you add a line to the crescent so that it makes a written “z” (for “zunehmend”, waxing), the Moon is waxing; if you get an “a” (for “abnehmend”, waning), it is waning. In the Southern Hemisphere, for example in Australia, it is exactly the other way round.

abschnitte.titel: When can you see the Moon?
abschnitte.text: The full moon rises at about sunset and sets at sunrise, so it can be seen all night long. The waxing half moon is in the sky in the evening. The waning half moon is seen mainly in the second half of the night and in the morning. That is why you can sometimes spot the Moon in the bright **daytime sky** too.

Thousands of years ago, people already based their calendars on the Moon. The word month comes from the word moon. The Islamic calendar is still a pure **lunar calendar** today. The date of Easter also depends on the Moon: Easter is on the Sunday after the first full moon in spring.

A **lunar eclipse** can only happen at full moon, when the Moon moves into the Earth’s shadow. A solar eclipse only happens at new moon, when the Moon covers the Sun. At new moon and full moon, the Sun and Moon pull on the oceans in a line. Then the tides are especially strong, which is called a spring tide.

begriffe.erklaerung: The phase of the Moon in which you cannot see the Moon, because its bright side faces away from us.
The phase of the Moon in which the Moon can be seen as a whole, bright disc.
The visible bright part of the Moon gets bigger from day to day.
The Moon moves into the Earth’s shadow and goes dark or reddish.

gewusst: A full moon near the horizon looks huge, even though it is the same size as when high in the sky.
At new moon the Moon is in the sky in the daytime with the Sun, we just cannot see it.
A full moon can sometimes occur twice in one calendar month; this is called a blue moon.

teile.einleitung: The mimosa is a plant that moves when you touch it. Its feathery leaves fold up in seconds. That is why it is also called the sensitive plant.
wichtigste: If you touch the leaves of the mimosa, they fold up.
After a few minutes they open again.
At night the leaves also fold up.
The mimosa produces small pink flowers that look like little balls.
It originally grows in Central and South America.
A very sensitive person is sometimes called a “mimosa”.

abschnitte.text: The leaves of the mimosa are made up of many small **leaflets**. If a leaf is touched, the leaflets fold together in pairs, and sometimes the whole leaf stalk droops. It happens amazingly fast. After **a few minutes** the leaves slowly stand up again. In botany, such a movement in response to touch or a shock is called **seismonasty**.

At the base of the leaves sit small swellings, the **pulvini**. Their cells are normally full of water. When touched, water quickly flows out of certain cells. This makes the pulvini go limp, and the leaf folds up. Later the cells fill up again, and the leaf opens.

Even without being touched, the leaves fold up **at night** and open again in the morning. This is called a **sleeping position**. Why the mimosa reacts to touch is not entirely clear. It probably serves as **protection from animals**: a folded leaf looks small and wilted and is less tempting to plant-eaters.

The mimosa produces small, **pink** flower heads that look like fluffy **little balls**. It belongs to the **legume family**, like peas and beans. It originally comes from **Central and South America**. Today it grows wild in many tropical countries. Here we keep it as a houseplant.

Because the plant reacts even to a light touch, a very **sensitive** person is described in German with the words “Er ist eine Mimose”, “He is a mimosa”. It means that someone is quickly hurt or offended. People also say “mimosenhaft”, meaning “mimosa-like”.

gewusst: The yellow, sweet-smelling flowers that florists often call “mimosas” are really acacias.
If you touch the mimosa many times in a row, it reacts more weakly as time goes on.

teile.einleitung: Cassava is a plant with thick, starchy root tubers. In many tropical countries it is an important staple food, but it is poisonous raw.
wichtigste: Cassava originally comes from the Amazon region of South America.
It is also called manioc or yuca.
Raw, it contains substances from which poisonous prussic acid can form.
Tapioca starch is obtained from cassava.
Fresh tubers go bad after just a few days.
In 2022 Nigeria harvested the most cassava.

abschnitte.text: **Cassava** was first grown in the **Amazon region** of South America. Portuguese sailors later brought it to **Africa** and **Asia**. It is also called **manioc** or, in Latin America, **yuca**. Its scientific name is Manihot esculenta, and it belongs to the **spurge family**, like the poinsettia.

Cassava contains substances from which poisonous **prussic acid** can form. That is why it must **not be eaten raw**. Peeling, soaking, boiling or roasting removes the poison. There is another problem: freshly harvested tubers often go bad after just **one to three days**. So they are processed quickly, for example into flour or dried pieces.

Almost pure **starch**, called **tapioca**, is obtained from the tubers. It is used to make, for example, the little balls in **bubble tea**. Tapioca is also used for puddings and for thickening dishes.

Cassava is very **hardy**. It also grows on poor soils and survives long **dry seasons**. The tubers can stay in the ground for a long time until they are needed. That is why cassava is an important staple food in many tropical countries. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, the **FAO**, **Nigeria** was the world’s biggest producer in 2022.
Farmers usually do not grow cassava from seeds. They stick pieces of the woody stem into the soil, called **cuttings**. New plants grow from these. Seeds are used almost only in **plant breeding**.

gewusst: For hundreds of millions of people in Africa, Asia and South America, cassava is a staple food.

teile.einleitung: Macronutrients are the nutrients that plants need in large amounts. They include nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulphur.
wichtigste: Plants need macronutrients in large amounts, but trace elements only in tiny amounts.
Nitrogen is the nutrient most needed by most crop plants.
Potassium controls the water balance and the stomata.
Magnesium sits at the centre of chlorophyll.
Sulphur is found in the amino acids cysteine and methionine.
NPK 15-15-15 means 15 per cent each of nitrogen, phosphate and potash.

abschnitte.text: Plants need nutrients in very different amounts. **Macronutrients** such as nitrogen, phosphorus, **potassium**, calcium, magnesium and sulphur are needed in large amounts. **Trace elements** such as boron, zinc and molybdenum are needed by the plant only in tiny amounts. The roots take up the nutrients as dissolved **ions** from the soil solution. Potassium, for example, is taken up as the singly positively charged **K+ ion**.

Plants build most of their mass from **carbon**, **hydrogen** and **oxygen**. These come from the CO2 in the air and from water, not from minerals in the soil. Together they make up over 90 per cent of the dry mass. Among the nutrients from the soil, **nitrogen** is the most important. It is found in all amino acids, proteins, nucleic acids and in chlorophyll.

**Potassium ions** regulate the osmotic pressure in the cells. In this way they control the opening and closing of the **stomata** and the water balance. Plants that get plenty of potassium suffer less from drought. **Magnesium** sits as the central atom in the ring-shaped **chlorophyll molecule**. Without magnesium, the plant cannot make chlorophyll.

**Sulphur** is a component of the amino acids **cysteine** and **methionine**, and so of many proteins. Oilseed rape and cabbage need an especially large amount of sulphur. **Calcium** strengthens cell walls and membranes. It is moved into the fruit only poorly inside the plant. In apples, a lack of calcium leads to **bitter pit**, with brown spots in the flesh.

abschnitte.titel: The numbers on a bag of fertiliser
abschnitte.text: Fertilisers often show **NPK** with three numbers, for example 15-15-15. The numbers give the share by mass in per cent: nitrogen as N, phosphate as P2O5 and potash as K2O. A 100 kg bag therefore contains 15 kg of each of these nutrients. The figures P2O5 and K2O are only values used for calculation; the plant takes up the substances as ions.

gewusst: If a plant lacks magnesium, its leaves often turn yellow between the veins.
Legumes such as clover can use nitrogen from the air with the help of bacteria.
